extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially those studying personal identity and moral philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Conceptual and forensic account of personal identity, consciousness, and types of relations (proportional, natural, instituted, moral), with attendant implications for responsibility, reward, and punishment. Extracts Locke's criteria for when sameness of person holds across change of substance, memory loss, and bodily change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity depends on consciousness, not substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal identity is constituted by the same consciousness: 'For it is by the consciousness it has of its present thoughts and actions, that it is SELF TO ITSELF now, and so will be the same self, as far as the same consciousness can extend to actions past or to come.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke repeatedly emphasizes that identity of the person is determined solely by continuity or sameness of consciousness across times, not by sameness of material or immaterial substance. Examples and thought experiments (sleep, interrupted consciousness, change of bodily parts, change of thinking substance) illustrate that the same consciousness uniting distant actions makes the same person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness alone unites remote existences into one person
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but consciousness can unite remote existences into the same person: without consciousness there is no person, and identity of substance alone will not do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke presents thought experiments (two incommunicable consciousnesses using same body; same consciousness inhabiting two bodies at intervals) to show that personhood follows where consciousness extends. This underpins accountability and moral responsibility: reward/punishment should track consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of the body are part of the self only while vitally united to consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Body-parts (limbs) are part of the self so long as they are vitally united to the thinking conscious self; when separated and no longer objects of that consciousness they cease to be part of the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: cut off a hand — once separated from the consciousness that experienced its sensations, it 'is then no longer a part of that which is himself.' This is used to illustrate that material continuity is not what grounds personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of thinking substance can preserve personal identity if consciousness transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same consciousness can be transferred from one thinking substance to another, then two distinct thinking substances may constitute one person, because personal identity follows the preserved consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke concedes that whether this is possible depends on the nature of thinking substances and whether consciousness is a transferrable representation. He invokes theological considerations (God's goodness) to rule out arbitrary transfers that would upset moral deserts, but leaves metaphysical possibility open pending clearer knowledge of thinking substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same immaterial substance without continuity of consciousness does not guarantee same person
rubrics_metrics.description: If an immaterial substance (soul) remains numerically the same but is wholly stripped of all consciousness of its past existence, it may constitute a different person; personal identity reaches no further than consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses examples of pre-existence and someone claiming to have been Socrates to show that numerical sameness of soul without remembered consciousness of past actions would not make one the same person for purposes of concern, account, or attribution of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The body contributes to 'man' even if personhood is consciousness-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the soul alone with its consciousness could make the same person across bodies, the body also goes to making what we call a 'man' — someone recognized socially/physically as the same human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes between 'person' (forensic, concerned with reward/punishment) and 'man' (the living human being identified by body and/or soul), noting that in ordinary language they overlap but analytically the body figures in our conception of the same man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons, not substances, are the objects of reward and punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Forensic responsibility (right and justice of reward and punishment) is founded on personal identity as determined by consciousness, not on identity of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that it is the conscious self that is concerned with happiness and misery, and thus moral and legal accountability should track the continuity of consciousness (the person), otherwise punishment without consciousness is tantamount to creating misery arbitrarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute oblivion separates actions from the person (but not from the man)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one wholly loses memory of some parts of one's life beyond retrieval, those actions fall outside the reach of the present person's consciousness and so are not properly theirs, though the same man may persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes legal and common practice (not punishing the mad for acts done when sober, etc.) that treats discontinuities of consciousness as splitting personhood. He distinguishes ordinary speech (where 'I' may still refer to the same man) from forensic identity grounded in memory/consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person is a forensic term
rubrics_metrics.description: PERSON is the name for the self as concerned with actions, merit, law, and happiness/misery; it belongs only to intelligent agents capable of law and moral accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke clarifies that personality extends beyond present existence to the past only by consciousness, since ownership and imputation of past actions depend on present appropriation via memory/consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of proportional relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportional relations arise when a simple idea capable of parts or degrees (e.g., whiteness, sweetness, equality, more) affords a way to compare subjects by that idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations depend on equality/excess of the same simple idea in different subjects and are sourced from sensation or reflection. Locke treats them as one class among many relational ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural relations are those founded on circumstances of origin or beginning (e.g., father/son, brothers, countrymen) and are as lasting as the subjects to which they belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes linguistic/practical reasons why humans have distinct names for such relations and observes that in non-human animals we typically do not mark these relations because of lesser social practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instituted or voluntary relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Instituted (voluntary) relations arise from acts by which someone acquires a moral right, power, or obligation (e.g., general/army, patron/client); they depend on human agreement and are alterable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations are reciprocal but sometimes overlooked due to naming conventions; they contrast with natural relations by being changeable through human will or social arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral relations (and moral rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral relations concern the conformity or disagreement of voluntary actions to a rule by which they are judged; moral good/evil is produced when such conformity or breach draws reward or punishment by the law-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke treats moral rules as a major class of relations and insists that for a rule to function as law it must have some enforcement (reward/punishment) beyond natural consequences. He ties moral good/evil to pleasure/pain as consequences and to the will/power of the lawgiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of laws that judge actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws men commonly refer actions to are: (1) Divine law, (2) Civil law, and (3) The law of opinion or reputation; by these laws actions are judged as sins/duties, criminal/innocent, or virtues/vices respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke enumerates these three sources of moral/legal judgment and indicates that each grounds different kinds of enforcement and social responses; he further argues that presuming a law without some annexed enforcement (reward/punishment) is implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law requires enforcement beyond natural consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule cannot properly function as law governing free agents unless some reward or punishment (not merely the natural consequence of the action) is annexed to it by the lawgiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke reasons that without an external enforcement mechanism, a supposed law would be ineffectual to determine will, since natural consequences alone would operate without need of a legislative rule.
